data.title: Hansen's disease (leprosy) — viva
data.summary: Leprosy & mycobacterial · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Hansen's disease (leprosy)** (Leprosy & mycobacterial)_

**Q1. What are the cardinal signs (WHO diagnostic criteria)?**
- At least one of: (1) definite loss of sensation in a pale (hypopigmented) or reddish skin patch; (2) thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness of muscles supplied by it; (3) presence of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear

**Q2. Classify leprosy.**
- Ridley–Jopling (immunological spectrum): TT, BT, BB, BL, LL, plus indeterminate and pure neuritic
- Indian (IAL 1981): indeterminate, tuberculoid, borderline, lepromatous, pure neuritic
- WHO operational: PB vs MB
- NLEP revised (2025): PB = 1–5 lesions, no nerve involvement, smear negative; MB = >5 lesions, OR any nerve involvement, OR smear positive

**Q3. Describe slit-skin smear technique and indices.**
- Pinch skin to blanch, 5 mm long 2–3 mm deep slit with No.15 blade, turn blade 90° and scrape, smear in circular manner, heat-fix, Ziehl–Neelsen (5% sulfuric acid decolourisation)
- Sites: ear lobes, eyebrows/forehead, chin, buttocks, active lesions (standard 4–6 sites)
- Bacteriological index (BI, Ridley logarithmic scale 0–6+), morphological index (% solid-staining bacilli — viability)

**Q4. Histopathology across the spectrum?**
- TT: epithelioid granulomas reaching epidermis, Langhans cells, nerve destruction, AFB nil
- BT: granulomas with clear subepidermal zone may be absent, few bacilli
- BB: epithelioid cells without giant cells, moderate bacilli
- BL: lymphocytes and foamy macrophages
- LL: Grenz zone, foamy (Virchow/lepra) cells, globi, plenty of bacilli

**Q5. Which nerves are thickened and how do you examine them?**
- Greater auricular, supraorbital, ulnar (most commonly), radial cutaneous, median, common peroneal (lateral popliteal), posterior tibial, sural, superficial peroneal
- Palpate for thickening, tenderness, consistency, nodularity, abscess; compare both sides; voluntary muscle testing and sensory testing (monofilament)

**Q6. Differential diagnosis of a hypopigmented patch?**
- Pityriasis alba, pityriasis versicolor, nevus depigmentosus/anaemicus, vitiligo (early), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, hypopigmented mycosis fungoides, sarcoidosis, PKDL — sensory loss distinguishes leprosy

**Q7. Causes of thickened nerves other than leprosy?**
- Hereditary motor sensory neuropathies (CMT type 1, Dejerine–Sottas, Refsum), neurofibromatosis, amyloidosis, acromegaly, primary amyloidosis, CIDP, sarcoidosis, nerve tumours

**Q8. What is MDT now (India)?**
- Since 1 April 2025 NLEP uses 3 drugs for both PB (6 months) and MB (12 months): adult rifampicin 600 mg + clofazimine 300 mg monthly supervised, clofazimine 50 mg + dapsone 100 mg daily; child 10–14 y: R 450, C 150 monthly, C 50 alternate days, D 50 daily; <10 y: R 10 mg/kg, C 100 mg monthly + 50 mg twice weekly, D 2 mg/kg

**Q9. Lepra reactions — types and treatment?**
- Type 1 (reversal, cell-mediated, BT/BB/BL): existing lesions inflamed, new lesions, neuritis — prednisolone 40 mg/day tapered over 12–20 weeks
- Type 2 (ENL, immune complex, BL/LL): crops of tender nodules, fever, neuritis, iritis, orchitis — NSAIDs (mild), prednisolone, thalidomide (drug of choice for recurrent), clofazimine 300 mg/day max 12 weeks
- Lucio phenomenon (diffuse LL, Mexico) — necrotising vasculitis

**Q10. Management of neuritis and disability?**
- Prednisolone for neuritis (silent neuritis too), splinting, physiotherapy; WHO disability grading 0/1/2; reconstructive surgery after 1 year of stable nerve function

**Q11. Prevention of trophic ulcers — '4 S'?**
- See (inspect daily), Soak, Scrape (callus), Smear (oil); MCR footwear; treat ulcers with rest, debridement, dressings

**Q12. Recent advances?**
- NLEP 3-drug regimen and revised classification (2025), single-dose rifampicin PEP for contacts, Mw/MIP vaccine, PCR/serology (anti-PGL-1), rifampicin resistance testing (rpoB), leprosy notification from all sectors

## Quick spotter facts
- Hypopigmented anaesthetic patch with thickened nerve — leprosy
- Leonine facies, madarosis — lepromatous leprosy

_Sources: DYP Survival Guide for PG Dermatology Exam (Long case — Hansen's disease); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch.138–149; NLEP 2025 revised regimen. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
